435.title: Hud and his people
435.hook: Hud tells 'Ad to ask forgiveness and He'll add strength to strength (11:52)
435.howItsDone: Muslim teachers encourage saying astaghfirullah, I ask God's forgiveness, often through the day, and cite Hud's words in 11:52 and Nuh's in 71:10–12 for the blessings tied to seeking forgiveness, including rain and strength.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Judi, where the ark came to rest, and your line, in his name it sails and anchors.
screen: `IN HIS NAME IT SAILS AND ANCHORS.`

segments.voice: You've met the people of 'Ad before, in al-A'raf: the tower builders of ancient Arabia, proud of their strength, and the prophet sent from among them, Hud. Surah Hud carries his name and gives his preaching more room. Here is a man standing up in a town where everyone is bigger, richer and louder than he is. They have wealth, fortresses, numbers; he has nothing they need. And he tells them that the way to grow even stronger is to do the one thing strong people find hardest.

Hud begins the way Nuh began before him in this surah: my people, worship God; you have no god but Him. I ask you no wage for this, he says; my wage is only from the One who made me. Then something that sounds almost like a business proposal, in verse fifty-two, in paraphrase: my people, ask forgiveness of your Lord, then turn back to Him. He will send the sky down on you in abundant rain, and add strength to your strength. Notice who he's talking to: not weak people, but a people already famous for strength. He doesn't tell them to give it up. He tells them how to get more. Here, asking forgiveness isn't a loss of face. It's a source of power. The rain matters too: for people in a dry land, rain is life. The same promise appears in another surah, on Nuh's lips: ask forgiveness, and He will send rain and help you with wealth and children. 'Ad answer: you've brought us no clear sign; we won't abandon our gods on your word. Some of our gods must have touched you with madness. Hud doesn't flinch. In paraphrase: I trust in God, my Lord and yours. There is no living creature He does not hold by its forelock. Commentators picture a horse led by the hair above its brow. Every creature, every tower builder, is held. In the end, the surah says, Hud and those with him were saved by a mercy from God, and 'Ad were followed by a curse in this world. The one thing the strong couldn't do, the thing that would have made them stronger, was to say: forgive me.

segments.voice: Think of one place where you've been holding on to being right, where saying sorry would feel like losing, and notice how much effort the holding takes. If you pray, you can say astaghfirullah slowly a few times, I ask God's forgiveness, and notice your shoulders; if not, rehearse in your mind the honest sorry you could say.

436.title: Salih's warning
436.hook: the camel is hamstrung, and three days later the cry comes (11:64–68)
436.howItsDone: Muslims retell the story of Salih as a lesson about honoring God's signs and showing mercy to animals, and many quote 11:61, 'my Lord is near, and answers,' when encouraging people to ask forgiveness.

segments.voice: Yesterday: 'Ad, the mighty people Hud warned. Your line was forgiveness is strength.

Every town has one: the bright kid everybody said would go far, the teachers, the neighbors, the aunties at weddings. Then one day the bright kid comes home and says something nobody wants to hear. Surah Hud keeps the words Thamud said to their prophet, Salih, and they sound exactly like that town: Salih, you were someone we had real hopes for, before this. You met Salih and the she-camel in al-A'raf. Surah Hud adds what he said before the camel, and what he said after.

Before. Verse sixty-one, in paraphrase: my people, worship God. He brought you out of the earth and settled you in it to build it up. So ask His forgiveness and turn to Him; my Lord is near, and answers. The phrase for settled you is ista'marakum, from the root of 'imara, building, cultivating, making a place live. They are the earth's tenants, not its owners. And God is described not as distant and angry, but as qarib, near, and mujib, the one who answers. Then their reply: we had hopes for you; are you forbidding us what our fathers worshiped? And Salih's answer, in verse sixty-three: if God has given me clear proof and mercy from Himself, who would help me against God if I disobeyed Him? You'd only add to my loss. Then the she-camel of God, a sign: let her graze, don't harm her. And after. They hamstrung her. Salih's last words, in verse sixty-five, are found only in this surah: enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days. That's a promise that won't be broken. Not a sudden blow. Three mornings in which a person could still turn, still weep, still ask the God who is near and answers. The surah doesn't say anyone did. On the third, the cry came, and they lay face down in their homes, as if they had never lived there. Salih and those with him were saved by a mercy from God, the verse says, from the disgrace of that day. Mercy came three ways: a near God, a gentle animal, three days of grace. Mercy was the test.

437.title: The guests and Lut
437.hook: the angels visit Ibrahim, then Lut's city is overturned (11:69–83)
437.howItsDone: Muslim teachers speak of hospitality to guests as part of faith, citing Ibrahim's welcome and Lut's protection of his guests, and the hadith 'whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honor his guest' (Sahih al-Bukhari).

segments.voice: Yesterday: Salih's warning, a near God and three days of grace. Your line was mercy was the test.

Last year you sat in Ibrahim's tent when the strangers came: the roasted calf, the hands that didn't reach for it, the laugh at the news of a son. Surah Hud follows those same guests out of the tent and down the road. Before they go, Ibrahim does something this path skipped then. He argues with them. He pleads for the people of the city they're heading to. Then the guests arrive at a second door, in that city, at dusk. And the man who opens it is filled with dread.

First, the pleading. Verse seventy-four says Ibrahim began to plead with God for the people of Lut, and verse seventy-five explains why: Ibrahim was forbearing, tender-hearted, always turning to God. The answer comes gently: Ibrahim, leave this; the command has come. Now the second door. The guests reach Lut's house, and verse seventy-seven says he was troubled for them, his heart tight: this is a hard day. He knows his city. Soon the men come rushing to his door, wanting his guests. The Qur'an names this city's wrongs in several surahs; in this telling, the heart of it is a crowd coming to seize a man's guests. Lut stands in his doorway and pleads: fear God, and don't shame me in my guests. Isn't there one right-minded man among you? There isn't. And Lut says something painfully honest, in verse eighty: if only I had strength against you, or could take refuge in some strong support. A host, alone, with nothing to protect his guests but his own body in the doorway. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ later said, in a hadith in Bukhari: may God have mercy on Lut; he was taking refuge in a strong support. He was, though he couldn't see it. The guests tell him: we are messengers from your Lord; they will not reach you. Leave in the last part of the night, and let no one look back, except your wife. At dawn the city is overturned. Two hosts: one fed strangers before he knew them; one stood in the door for them. Hospitality protects.

438.title: Only reform
438.hook: Shu'ayb says: I want only reform, as far as I am able, and my success is from Allah (11:88)
438.howItsDone: Some Muslims write or say wa ma tawfiqi illa billah, my success comes only from God, from 11:88, at the start of a book, a thesis or a new venture, and scholars cite Shu'ayb's words as a model for anyone working for reform.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lut, and two hosts who guarded strangers. Your line was hospitality protects.

A short line of Arabic sometimes sits on the first page of a Muslim student's thesis, or above the desk in a family shop: wa ma tawfiqi illa billah. My success comes only from God. It's from the Qur'an. What's easy to miss is who said it first, and what kind of day he was having. It was Shu'ayb, the prophet of Madyan, the town with the crooked scales you met in al-A'raf. He was being mocked. And the line was half of his answer.

Madyan had sneered: Shu'ayb, does your prayer tell you how we should spend our own money? His answer in verse eighty-eight has three parts. First, in paraphrase: I don't want to go behind your backs and do the very thing I'm forbidding you. No hidden deal, no double standard. Second, in Pickthall's translation: "I desire naught save reform so far as I am able." And third: my success comes only from God; in Him I trust, and to Him I turn. The key word is islah. Its root, s-l-h, means to be sound, whole, working the way it should. The prophet Salih, two days ago, carries the same root in his name. The root also gives sulh, reconciliation, making peace between two people. So islah is repair: of a scale, a market, a friendship. Notice what Shu'ayb doesn't claim. Not: I'll fix everything. As far as I am able. And the results aren't his to own. Then Surah Hud keeps going, past the line that ends up on the walls. Verse eighty-nine: don't let your quarrel with me push you into wrong. Verse ninety: ask forgiveness; my Lord is merciful, loving, wadud. And their answer, verse ninety-one: we don't understand much of what you say, and if it weren't for your clan, we'd have stoned you. Shu'ayb replies: is my clan more honored by you than God? Even with threats on the table, the reformer stays honest, modest about his reach, and points past himself.

If you pray, you can say his words: my success comes only from God.

439.title: The best of stories
439.hook: We tell you the best of stories (12:3)
439.howItsDone: Surah Yusuf is often retold; parents tell it to children, and teachers use it to speak about patience, temptation and forgiveness within families.

segments.voice: Yesterday: islah, Shu'ayb's repair, as far as he was able. Your line was only to set things right.

Surah Hud ended with prophet after prophet, and people after people who would not listen. It's heavy. The next surah opens differently, like someone settling into a chair by the fire. We tell you, it says, the best of stories. You've met Yusuf already on this path: the dream of the eleven stars, the well, the prison, the palace. Now, back to him with a different question. Not what happens. Why does this surah open by speaking of the best of stories?
screen: `WE TELL YOU THE BEST OF STORIES.`

segments.voice: Verse three, in Pickthall's translation, begins: "We narrate unto thee (Muhammad) the best of narratives". In Arabic, ahsan al-qasas. Qasas can mean the stories themselves or the act of telling them, so commentators read it both ways: the best of stories, or the best way of telling. They also differ on what it points to: the story of Yusuf that follows, or the Qur'an's telling as a whole. Some commentators place the surah in a hard stretch of the Prophet's years in Mecca, around the time he lost his wife Khadija and his uncle Abu Talib, with the small community under heavy pressure. And here is a story about a boy betrayed by his brothers, sold, slandered, jailed, forgotten, who ends up with power over the very people who wronged him. So what makes it best? Commentators give answers that stack. It's complete: one prophet's story told from beginning to end in a single surah. It has every kind of person: prophets and kings, a jealous family, a woman who tries to seduce and later confesses, a prisoner, a merchant, a grieving father. It has every kind of trial: envy, temptation, injustice, long separation, grief that whitens a father's eyes. And it ends not in destruction, like the stories in Hud, but in a family reunited and a sentence of forgiveness. When the brothers finally stand before him, Yusuf says: no reproach on you today. The best of stories is the one where the wronged man, with all the power in the room, chooses mercy.

segments.voice: Run Yusuf's story in five pictures, one per breath: the dream, the well, the prison, the palace, the brothers bowing. Then go back to the picture you feel most, and stay with it a while. Let it end where Yusuf ends it: no reproach on you today.
Ahsan al-qasas. The phrase that opens the story of Yusuf, read as the best of stories or the best way of telling.
Your line: no reproach on you today. Said by the man holding all the power. Thanks for sitting with me.

440.title: Reading it whole
440.hook: the only prophet's story told complete in one surah
440.tomorrow: A lesson for those with minds
440.howItsDone: Some Muslims read Surah Yusuf straight through, at home or in study circles, and teachers point out its patterns: the dream that opens and closes it, the shirt that appears three times, and Ya'qub's 'beautiful patience.'

segments.voice: Yesterday: ahsan al-qasas, the best of stories, where the wronged man with all the power chooses mercy.

Musa's story in the Qur'an is everywhere. A scene in al-Baqarah, a long stretch in al-A'raf, his childhood in Ta Ha, his journey with a mysterious teacher in al-Kahf, Pharaoh's last words in Yunus. You put it together like a puzzle, across the whole book. Many prophets' stories are told that way, each surah taking the piece it needs. Yusuf is different. One surah, a hundred and eleven verses, beginning, middle and end. It can be read the way a novel is read: whole, in one sitting, so you can see its shape.

Read it whole, and patterns appear that you'd never catch in pieces. Start with the frame. Near the beginning, a boy tells his father a dream: eleven stars, the sun and the moon, bowing to him. Near the end, his parents and his brothers bow before him, and Yusuf says: this is the meaning of my dream from long ago. The whole surah lives between the telling of one dream and its coming true. Then watch the shirt. It appears three times. First, the brothers bring it home stained with false blood, to tell their father a wolf ate him. Second, in Egypt, it's torn from behind, and the tear proves Yusuf was running away, not toward. Third, Yusuf sends it home, and when it's laid on his blind father's face, his sight comes back. A lie, then the truth, then healing, all through the same piece of cloth. Then listen to the father. When the brothers come home with the bloody shirt, Ya'qub says: sabrun jamil, beautiful patience, the line you carried last year. Years later, when another son is held in Egypt, he says it again. Twice, in the worst moments. Commentators describe it as patience without complaint to people, while still pouring out grief to God, which Ya'qub does. None of this jumps out from one verse. A dream that closes, a shirt that changes meaning, a phrase that returns. You only see the design when you read it whole.
screen: `A DREAM, AND ITS COMING TRUE.` · `THE SHIRT, THREE TIMES.` · `A LIE, THE TRUTH, THEN HEALING.` · `BEAUTIFUL PATIENCE, TWICE.` · then, large: `READ IT WHOLE.`

segments.voice: If you pray, begin with bismillah. Then picture the three appearances of the shirt, one per breath: false blood, torn from behind, laid on a father's face. Hold the last one longest, the same cloth, now healing.
Sabrun jamil. Beautiful patience, the phrase Ya'qub says twice in Surah Yusuf, patience without complaint to people while grief pours out to God. Today's word.
Your line: read it whole. A shape only shows from far enough back. See you tomorrow.

441.title: A lesson for those with minds
441.hook: in their stories is a lesson for people of understanding (12:111)
441.howItsDone: Muslim teachers close a study of Surah Yusuf with 12:111 and ask students to draw lessons, 'ibar, from the story for their own lives; the phrase ulu al-albab recurs throughout the Qur'an for people of reflection.

segments.voice: Yesterday: reading Surah Yusuf whole, the shirt three times, sabrun jamil said twice. And that's the end of a week.

What are stories for? This week was a parade of people. The mighty 'Ad, told that forgiveness is strength. Thamud and the she-camel. Ibrahim's roasted calf and Lut in his doorway. Shu'ayb and the honest scales. Then Yusuf, the best of stories, read whole. The very last verse of Surah Yusuf answers the question, and not just for Yusuf. It looks back over everything, the prophets of Surah Hud included, and says what a reader is supposed to do with a story once it's over.

Verse one hundred eleven, in Pickthall's translation: "In their history verily there is a lesson for men of understanding." Two Arabic words carry it. The first is 'ibra, a lesson. Its root, '-b-r, means to cross over, the way you cross a river; 'ubur is a crossing. The same root gives ta'bir, the interpreting of dreams, which runs all through this surah: Yusuf crosses from the picture in the dream to what it means. So an 'ibra is a lesson you get by crossing over, from their story to your life. The second word is albab, minds, the plural of lubb: the core of a thing, the kernel inside the shell. Ulu al-albab, people with minds, are people who get to the core. The verse goes on: this isn't an invented tale, but a confirmation of what came before it, a detailed explanation of everything, and a guidance and a mercy for people who believe. So the Qur'an doesn't tell stories just to pass the evening, or to make you wonder how it ends. It tells them so you'll cross over. Yusuf's brothers, jealous of a favored child: is there a jealousy in your house? The woman who lied, then confessed: is there a truth you've been holding back? A father who said beautiful patience twice: what are you waiting through right now? The story is told so the one hearing it can step into it, and come out somewhere else.
screen: `'IBRA — A LESSON, A CROSSING.` · `TA'BIR — INTERPRETING DREAMS.` · `LUBB — THE CORE, THE KERNEL.` · `FROM THEIR STORY TO YOUR LIFE.` · then, large: `THE STORY IS THE LESSON.`

segments.voice: Let the story pass in front of you: the dream, the well, the house, the prison, the palace, the brothers bowing. Where does it touch your life? Let one lesson come, in a single plain sentence of your own; if you pray, ask to understand it.
'Ibra. A lesson you cross over into, from their story to your life, the word that closes Surah Yusuf. Today's word.
Your line: the story is the lesson. Their story, crossed over into yours. Day four hundred forty-one, and a week complete.
